claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native surface oxide layer formed under ambient conditions.
Exposure to salt-laden environments at 700–900 °C induces a phase transformation in the native oxide on Q235 steel.
The high-temperature phase transformation converts the native oxide from a dense, adherent film into a porous, less-protective scale.
The transformed high-temperature oxide scale spalls from Q235 steel.
Under room-temperature salt exposure, the native oxide remains amorphous and coherent.
The coherent room-temperature oxide retains limited corrosion protection.
High-temperature transformation may produce Fe2O3 or non-protective spinel variants.
Differences in oxide-phase volumetric expansion and stability cause porosity, reduced adhesion, and spallation.
Porosity and spallation accelerate corrosion by exposing the underlying Q235 steel.
At room temperature, the absence of oxide phase transformations permits slow, self-passivating oxide growth.
Salt-exposed Q235 samples treated at 700–900 °C will show significantly greater mass change than salt-exposed room-temperature samples.
Salt-exposed Q235 samples treated at 700–900 °C will show more oxide porosity and spallation than room-temperature samples.
XRD will detect oxide microstructural or phase transformations in the high-temperature samples relative to the room-temperature samples.
Room-temperature salt-exposed samples will exhibit only minor mass change and a relatively intact oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to Q235 steel that has been pre-annealed, alloyed, or otherwise modified to improve high-temperature passivation.
